grammarPoints.title: Noun sentences with は and です
grammarPoints.meaning: Use a polite noun predicate to identify or describe the topic: X is Y. Japanese often leaves the topic unspoken when the situation makes it clear. Nouns do not take English-style a/an or plural endings; context supplies that meaning.
grammarPoints.formation: (X は) Y です. は marks the topic and is pronounced wa in this use. です follows the noun or noun phrase.
notes: は marks what the sentence is about, not necessarily its grammatical subject.
The affirmative nonpast pattern is introduced here; noun negation and past forms appear in later lessons.
Use names and titles naturally; speakers commonly omit a clear topic and address a listener by name or title rather than あなた.
Use さん after another person’s name, never after your own. 先生 normally describes someone else; 教師 is a modest way to state your own teaching profession.

grammarPoints.title: Polite questions and question words
grammarPoints.meaning: Turn a polite statement into a yes-or-no question with か. For a question-word question, put the needed question word in the corresponding noun or value position and keep the polite sentence frame.
grammarPoints.formation: Polite statement + か. Wh-question: topic は question word ですか, or topic は question word + counter/time expression ですか.
notes: A Japanese question normally does not need a question mark in standard printed text.
Japanese は in the topic position is pronounced wa.
Read 何 as なん immediately before です and these counters: 何時 (なんじ), 何歳 (なんさい), 何年生 (なんねんせい), 何番 (なんばん). Before many particles it is なに; 何人 meaning “what nationality” is なにじん.
When answering, the listener can omit a repeated topic when it is obvious.

grammarPoints.title: Connecting nouns with の
grammarPoints.meaning: の links two nouns to show ownership, affiliation, origin, or another close relationship. The second noun names the main thing; the first narrows whose or what kind it is.
grammarPoints.formation: Noun 1 の Noun 2. Treat the complete phrase as one noun phrase wherever a noun can appear.
notes: The English relationship may be possessive (‘Aki’s bag’) or descriptive (‘a student of biology’); の does not always translate as English of.
The rightmost noun is the head of the phrase.
